implementation_notes: In process the splitter is a LINQ projection: SelectMany projects one composite into many parts (flatMap) and Enumerable.Chunk (net6.0+, C# 10) groups a sequence into fixed-size parts when the channel wants batches, so no role structure is written at all - the send loop stays an ordinary await foreach. For byte-level framing the same loop runs over an IAsyncEnumerable<T> decoder, and System.Threading.Channels or Parallel.ForEachAsync take the place of the framework's dispatcher. The classic component form earns its keep only where a platform owns the topology (see the Durable Functions variant); otherwise a hand-written Splitter class is ceremony around a foreach.
pitfalls: LINQ operators are deferred: building the projection inside the publish loop re-enumerates the source and emits duplicate parts.
Chunk throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for size < 1, and the last chunk is short (only the last one) - consumers must not assume equal part sizes.
Fire-and-forget publishes (or async void handlers) inside the loop drop ordering and swallow failures; await each publish or collect the tasks first.
Sequence headers must be per-composite state: a counter field on a singleton service produces colliding correlation metadata.

variants.name: Durable Functions fan-out/fan-in orchestrator
variants.idiom_name: orchestrator CallActivityAsync per element + Task.WhenAll fan-in
variants.implementation_notes: When the split must be durable and distributed, the platform owns the roles: an orchestrator calls the activity once per element (the fan-out), collects the tasks and awaits Task.WhenAll (the fan-in), and the runtime checkpoints every call so a crash replays the split instead of losing parts. This is the closest .NET equivalent of a framework-native Splitter/Aggregator pair, and it also supplies the concurrency across machines that a plain loop cannot. Keep the classic in-process loop for splits that need no durability, and keep the orchestrator free of the splitting logic itself.
pitfalls: Orchestrator code must be deterministic and replay-safe: schedule activities instead of doing I/O, clocks or Guid.NewGuid() in the orchestrator.
Fanning out over an unbounded collection grows the orchestration history; page or throttle the split.
Task.WhenAll fails fast while the remaining activities keep running - decide explicitly whether to cancel or compensate.
Awaiting each call inside the loop serialises the fan-out and removes the reason to use an orchestrator.
